name: Freya Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the stockperson for the hens at Kettle Lane Farm, which the Dawson family run. Twelve thousand free-range layers in three sheds, plus about a hundred and fifty hectares of wheat and maize that the brothers mostly look after. I'm in at half six, walk every shed, check water lines, feeders, any dead or poorly birds, then let them out to range and spend the morning on the egg packing side. Hens are funny. You'd be surprised how much personality twelve thousand of anything can have.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about outside work, and how you get by?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single and I rent a flat above the bakery on Mill Street, so I wake up to bread, which is a perk. I've got about five months' worth saved, because I'm a bit careful like that. I use the AI app on my phone now and again, mostly to check a feed ration sum or tidy up an email to the egg buyer, but I'm not the type to try every new thing; I let someone else go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and probably no one would be very surprised. I'd tell the Dawsons it was worth trying a couple of the tools, but we didn't need to change much. Online I'd stay out of it, I don't really argue on there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's about what I expected. The egg collection on the farm already went automatic years ago, belts that bring the eggs to the packing room, and that didn't get rid of me. A bit more help with the paperwork would be nice, but it wouldn't change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Kettle Lane, keep saving, and maybe use the AI app a bit more for the flock records, now the others have figured out which bits are useful. I'd think about the poultry welfare course at the college, because the supermarkets keep asking for more checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fine, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the egg belts didn't get rid of you. What changed when they came in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before my time they had two people collecting by hand, and when the belts came in one went to the packing room and one retired. It was gentle, nobody lost out badly. That's how I imagine change, if I'm honest, even when people make a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the job would you most like a bit of help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The audit paperwork. Every month there's a form for the supermarket, the welfare people and the egg board, and they all want the same numbers in different boxes. If AI could fill those in, I'd buy it a cake from downstairs.

S0.say: I'd say that's that then, and nobody would be very surprised. I'd tell the farm family it was worth trying a few tools but we didn't need to change much.
S0.think: It's about what I expected, because the egg collection went automatic years ago and that didn't get rid of me. A bit more help with paperwork would be nice but not life-changing.
S0.do: Carries on at Kettle Lane Farm and keeps saving. Uses the AI app a bit more for flock records once others have found the useful parts, and considers the poultry welfare course at the college.
S0.quote: If AI could fill those in, I'd buy it a cake from downstairs.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is grounded and unbothered by the calm scenario. Her picture of change comes from the egg belts on her own farm, which shifted jobs without hurting anyone. She wants help with audit paperwork, which she described with real exasperation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll mean a lot of change but people will adjust, like they did with the egg belts. At work I'd say we should look at what's actually working on other poultry farms before buying anything. I'd be the sensible one in the room, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've seen the videos of robots that roll up and down poultry sheds checking the birds and picking up floor eggs. If those got cheap and reliable, the shed walking, which is a big part of my job, could go. I'd still be needed for the hands-on stuff, but maybe they'd need me fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the Dawsons to let me see a robot on another farm, and if it worked, I'd want to be the one who learns to run it. I'd keep up the savings and maybe push to six months. I'd also do the poultry welfare course properly, because a robot can't sign off a welfare audit, at least not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A low hum in the back of my mind, but nothing I can't handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust one of those shed robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it on a farm like ours for a full flock, about fourteen months. The Dawsons' cousin has a big unit in the next valley; if he had one and it didn't scare the birds or miss a dead one, I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they might need you fewer hours. How would that hit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was four days instead of five, I'd survive, I've got the savings and the rent's not huge. If it went to three, I'd need to find something else on the side, maybe helping at the bakery downstairs, which they've asked me about anyway.

S1.say: I'd say it means a lot of change but people will adjust, like with the egg belts. At work I'd say let's look at what's working on other poultry farms before buying anything.
S1.think: I've seen robots that patrol poultry sheds checking birds and picking up floor eggs. If they got cheap and reliable, the shed walking could go and the farm might need me for fewer hours.
S1.do: Asks her employers to show her a shed robot on another farm and, if it works, offers to learn to run it. Pushes savings towards six months and takes the poultry welfare course, since audits still need a person to sign off.
S1.feel: Uneasy, a low hum in the background that she can handle.
S1.quote: A robot can't sign off a welfare audit, at least not yet.
S1.fieldNote: Freya knows exactly which part of her job is exposed: the shed walking. She wants to see proof over a full flock before trusting a robot, but would then volunteer to run it. Fewer hours worries her more than outright job loss, and she already has a fallback at the bakery below her flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government needs to steady things, maybe help with wages while people retrain. I wouldn't be marching, that's not me, but I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan. At work I'd say let's not panic, let's see what the Dawsons can afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think, honestly, it'd be the end of my job inside a couple of years. If the robots can do everything in a hen shed, the Dawsons would have to buy them, because the big egg producers would, and they'd undercut us. I'm not the person who leaps first, and in two years there's no time to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back right away, no holidays, and keep all five months in the bank. I'd ask around, my sister in the city works for a delivery company, about anything going there. If I lost the job, I'd probably give up the flat and move in with her for a bit while I sorted myself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be doing sums in my head on the walk to the sheds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in with your sister. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Odd, at twenty-nine, on her sofa with her two cats. She'd be lovely about it, she always is. But I'd miss the bakery smell and the hens, and I'd feel like I'd gone backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not the one who leaps first. What happens to people like you when there's no time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we get left behind, to be blunt. The ones who jumped early would be running the robots, and I'd be reading about it. That's the bit that makes me cross with myself, a little.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast and the government needs to steady things, maybe by supporting wages while people retrain. I wouldn't march, but I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan.
S2.think: I think my job would be gone within a couple of years, because big egg producers would buy the robots and undercut us. I'm not someone who leaps first, and there'd be no time to wait and see.
S2.do: Cuts spending straight away and keeps all five months of savings in the bank. Asks her sister about work at a delivery company in the city, and if she loses her job, gives up the flat and moves in with her sister while she sorts herself out.
S2.feel: Anxious, doing sums on the walk to the sheds, and a little cross with herself for being slow to move.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I'd gone backwards.
S2.fieldNote: Freya's usual approach of letting others go first doesn't work with two years' warning, and she knows it. Her savings and her sister give her a soft landing, which keeps her anxious rather than panicked. Her frustration is mostly with herself, not with anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, if farms and colleges work together. I'd say to the others, keep your eyes open and don't spend money you might need. I'd probably share the odd article in the farm group chat, but nothing preachy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see it as my warning to get moving. I'd watch for a year or two, see how fast the robots spread on poultry farms, and then make a move before I'm pushed. I'd be thirty-two at the end, which feels fine for a change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the welfare course in the first year, then look at becoming a farm assurance inspector, the people who visit farms and check standards, because someone has to visit and look, even if robots run the sheds. I'd keep the savings at about six months. And I'd use the AI tools more as other people show me how, so I'm not behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More time means less fear, but it's still a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't inspection get automated too, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, eventually. But I think people will still want a human to say, yes, I stood in that shed and it was fine. Supermarkets love a signature. I could be wrong, but it's my best guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the Dawsons, if you started planning to leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them early, that's only fair, they've been decent to me. Probably over tea in Mrs Dawson's kitchen, with the dog under the table. I'd offer to train whoever comes next, or help set up the robots if that's where they go.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but workable if farms and colleges work together. I'd tell colleagues to keep their eyes open and not spend money they might need.
S3.think: I'd see it as my warning to get moving: watch for a year or two, then move before I'm pushed. At thirty-two a change feels fine.
S3.do: Takes the poultry welfare course in the first year, then works towards becoming a farm assurance inspector. Keeps about six months saved, uses AI tools more as others show her how, and tells her employers early if she plans to leave.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with less fear but still a deadline.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Freya's way of working: watch, then move before she's pushed. She bets that people will still want a human signature on farm inspections, while admitting she could be wrong. Her loyalty to the farm family shows in how she'd tell them early and offer to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say there's no need for panic, just steady planning. I'd say it to anyone who asked: pick a direction in the next few years and work towards it. I'd probably be the calm voice in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be fine. Ten years is longer than I've been on the farm. I've already changed once, from working in a supermarket at nineteen to this, so I know I can do it when I have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Kettle Lane for most of it, do the welfare course and then the inspector training over a few years. I'd keep saving, and I'd probably put some of it towards buying a small flat, since a decade is long enough to plan that. When robots started arriving on poultry farms, I'd volunteer to learn them so I had that experience too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like seeing a big job on the list for next year, not for this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you changed once already. What was that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scary for about a month. I'd done three years on the tills, and I took a pay cut for the farm apprenticeship. My mum thought I was mad. But I'd been planning it for a year, and that's why it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in the ten-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Dawson, actually. He's in his sixties and he loves those hens more than he lets on. If the farm went full robot, I think it'd take something out of him. But that's his choice to make, not mine.

S4.say: I'd say there's no need for panic, just steady planning: pick a direction in the next few years and work towards it. I'd be the calm voice in the group chat.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine, because ten years is longer than I've been on the farm. I already changed careers once, from a supermarket job to farming, so I know I can do it with time.
S4.do: Stays at Kettle Lane Farm for most of the decade while doing the welfare course and then inspector training. Keeps saving and puts some towards buying a small flat, and volunteers to learn the shed robots when they arrive.
S4.feel: Calm, like a big job on next year's list rather than this afternoon's.
S4.quote: I took a pay cut for the farm apprenticeship. My mum thought I was mad.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years plays to Freya's strengths: she changes well when she can plan ahead, as she did when she left supermarket work. She'd even consider buying a flat. Her concern turns to her older employer and what full automation would take out of him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. I'm someone who needs time to see what works, and that one takes the time away. What would help is wage support for a while, and short, practical courses, run by the college or the farm assurance people, so you can switch without going broke.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what customers want. People pay extra for free-range eggs because they picture a person in a field with the hens. If it's all robots, will they still pay? I don't know. It's the question I'd ask if I were the Dawsons.

headlineQuote: People pay extra for free-range eggs because they picture a person in a field with the hens. If it's all robots, will they still pay?
portrait: Freya Farah is 27 and looks after 12,000 free-range hens at Kettle Lane, a family poultry and arable farm, living alone in a rented flat above a bakery with about five months saved. She's practical, uses AI apps now and then, and waits to see a thing work before she trusts it. Her sense of change comes from the egg belts that shifted jobs on her farm without hurting anyone. Only the two-year AGI picture makes her anxious, because it gives her no time to watch and plan, and she'd lean on her sister if the job went. With five or ten years she plans steady training towards farm inspection work, drawing confidence from having already changed careers once.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because she needs time to see what works and that version takes the time away.
whatWouldHelp: Wage support for a while and short, practical courses from the college or farm assurance bodies, so people can switch without going broke.
